title: Wave patterns in two-dimensional networks of non-locally coupled oscillators with phase delay
abstract: We studied the wave patterns in non-locally, repulsively coupled oscillators on a 2D lattice. The repulsive coupling is tuned by the phase delay $απ$ and the wave patterns are found in the regime $α\in \left[0.5, 1\right]$. We focused on the growth of orientationally correlated domains and found that the average total boundary size $\overline{|B|}$ obeys an approximate power law $\overline{|B|}\propto t^{-b}$ for $α= 0.8$ and $α=0.9$. In contrast, at $α= 0.7$, the dynamics is disrupted by defect-mediated domain formation and domain splitting. The fitting-window dependence of the apparent exponent $b$, as well as the mean and standard deviation of the wave speed $c$, decreases with increasing $α$, which is consistent with the linear stability analysis of the wave solution.
summary: This paper analyzes wave patterns in 2D lattices of oscillators coupled non-locally with a tunable phase delay $\alpha$. It finds that the system undergoes distinct dynamic regimes: stable coarsening occurs for higher $\alpha$, while lower values induce domain splitting mediated by topological defects. The work uses LSA and numerical simulations to map out this transition based on the coupling parameter.
main_problem: The study investigates wave patterns, domain coarsening dynamics, and defect formation in a 2D lattice of non-locally coupled oscillators influenced by a phase delay parameter.
main_result: Coarsening (power-law decay of boundary size) is observed for specific phase delays ($\alpha \in [0.8, 1]$), while lower values ($\alpha=0.7$) exhibit qualitative changes marked by domain splitting and defect mediation.
method: The research combines linear stability analysis (LSA) to study planar wave solutions with extensive numerical simulations of the coupled oscillator dynamics.
model_or_system: The system is a square lattice of identical phase oscillators whose evolution is governed by a non-local coupling term dependent on the phase delay $\alpha$. The dynamics are analyzed in a rotating frame, simplifying the governing equation.
key_observables: Average total boundary size ($\overline{|B|}$), domain coarsening exponent ($b$), wave speed ($c$), and winding number (defect quantification).
important_parameters: The phase delay parameter $\alpha$, which controls the repulsive nature of the coupling, is critical; regimes are compared for $\alpha=0.7, 0.8,$ and $0.9$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on approximating domain growth via power-law scaling ($|B|\propto t^{-b}$) and assumes the validity of planar traveling-wave solutions for LSA.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate snapshots showing wave domain emergence/coarsening (Fig. 2), time evolution of boundary size confirming power-law decay for high $\alpha$ (Fig. 4), and visualizations of defect structures using winding numbers (Fig. 3c).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical model and governing equations, through applying LSA to characterize stable wave solutions, to presenting numerical simulations that track domain evolution and boundary size decay across different values of the phase delay $\alpha$.
why_interesting: The study models complex non-equilibrium pattern formation (coarsening/domain splitting) in a system exhibiting collective dynamics, which shares mathematical parallels with critical phenomena and phase transitions studied in statistical mechanics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Linear stability diagram for q-twisted states for this system with α > 0.5. The blue dots mark vectors (qx, qy) ∈[−256, 255] for which every nonzero perturbation κ has a negative growth rate. The anisotropic shape reflects the discreteness and fourfold symmetry of the square lattice.

FIG. 2. Snapshots of the oscillator phases ϕij for a system with α = 0.8. Each pixel represents one oscillator on the two- dimensional lattice with the color representing the phase ϕij. The panels show (a) the random initial condition at t = 0, (b) t = 1280, (c) t = 12800, and (d) t = 51200. Locally coherent traveling-wave domains emerge and coarsen over time.

FIG. 3. (a-c) show various snapshots of the same sample (with α = 0.8) at the same time t = 51200 as Fig. 2(d). (a) shows the magnitude of the local average phase-gradient vector |⟨(∇ϕ)ij⟩|. (b) shows the calculated boundary region of that snapshot in black. (c) shows the winding number wij (blue positive, red negative). An isolated defect with total winding number w = 1 is marked with a black circle. (c) only displays values in the bottom right quadrant for better visibility. (d) shows the relative frequency of |⟨(∇ϕ)ij⟩| for 25600 ≤t ≤51200 for all α. The threshold λ = 0.7 used to distinguish between boundary and non-boundary regions is marked by a dashed black line.

FIG. 5. Histogram for the absolute wave speed c for the range 25600 ≤t ≤51200. Both mean and variance increase with decreasing α. The wave speed is calculated from the gra- dient and the phase velocity cij = |Ωij| |∇ϕij| with Ωij = d dtϕij(t). The shaded regions indicate theoretical wave-speed ranges for idealized planar waves obtained from the linear stability anal- ysis, used here as reference ranges. The observed peaks fall within their respective ranges. Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Material validates the numerical wave-speed calculation by comparing idealized planar-wave simulations with the theo- retical planar-wave speed.

FIG. 4. (a) shows the time evolution of the average total boundary size for each α. The average is taken from all 20 samples for each α. The shaded area indicates the sample- to-sample standard deviation. The range 3200 ≤t < 51200 has been fitted with At−b. The exponent is shown on the graph. The power-law decay is clearly visible for α = 0.8 and α = 0.9. The fitted exponents are b0.8 = 0.30 ± 0.04 and b0.9 = 0.377 ± 0.008.
